https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ym.text: Figure caption, Watch: Teacher saved the lives of 900 students after phone call By Ashok Dahal and Kamal Pariyar, BBC Nepali Reporting from Nuwakot district Published 30 August 2026, 17:10 BST Updated 3 hours ago A headteacher has told how he saved 900 pupils' lives from the Nepal floods - by quickly evacuating them just 10 minutes before the waters hit. Rajendra Dawadi, who is in charge of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, told the BBC he had received four calls at 09:10 local time (03:25 GMT) warning about the disaster, which has now claimed at least 794 lives. He quickly decided to evacuate, telling the children to run to higher ground and ordering buses full of students to turn around to flee the area. Dawadi said: "If we didn't make a quick decision, if it was 10 minutes later, we all - including the students and me - wouldn't be able to speak to you today." What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods Published 9 hours ago The warnings had come from four different people in the space of minutes and helped him evaluate the impending danger. "A parent came and told me that 'a big flood was coming, I am here to take my daughter, I will take her'," he added. "Parents don't rush without a strong reason, so it was confirmed that I shouldn't waste a second to evacuate the children. "I decided I shouldn't delay any more. Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day's classes. "I feel proud that we saved so many lives." The floods - which decimated parts of Nepal on Wednesday and have left at least 2,426 people missing - saw the school building buried under mud and debris. Dawadi said the waters arrived so quickly that a hostel building about 100m (328ft) from the river was engulfed immediately. Image caption, Pupil Yunisha Amatya, 16, managed to get to safety with just moments to spare At first, many students did not realise how serious the situation was. Pupil Yunisha Amatya, 16, said she scrambled to safety with her friends just before the flood hit. "I along with my friends survived by just 10 seconds only," she told the BBC. "Just before the flood came, we were in the class studying. Teachers had gathered in one place and initially had no idea what had happened. After five minutes teachers came and informed us about the flood and asked us to go home." She said one student fainted after hearing about the disaster, but many initially underestimated the danger and waited for classmates who were in a maths lesson. Yunisha and her friends scrambled uphill through an escape route behind the school. "I could not walk fast, and my friends helped me to climb uphill. We tried our best to be in the safer zones then. We escaped through a narrow ladder from backside of the school. Within no time, the bazaar was swept away in front of my eyes," she says, referring to the local market around the school. "If there was no grip in my shoes I would have fallen and students and other people were jostling each other to reach the safer area while escaping. The people who choose to escape from another route are apparently swept away." Students and teachers initially moved a few hundred metres uphill to safety before making their way to a neighbouring village. With roads cut off and transport disrupted, many remained stranded for two nights before rescue efforts reached them. The principal and Yunisha, who both live across the river from the school, were eventually airlifted back to their home village. Meanwhile parents were desperately trying to contact their children and relatives. Yunisha's mother, Sabina Kumari Shrestha, says she repeatedly tried to call both her daughter and husband, but neither could be reached. Her husband, Yubaraj Amatya, immediately headed towards the school. "Soon after the flood news spread, I tried my daughter's number, but she was not reachable, then I was afraid," he said. "Within a few minutes I rushed toward my daughter's school and Trishuli Bazar was all swept by the flood, then I thought my daughter was no more. I was so horrified, stopped my scooter, there was flooding but I could not think of returning without my daughter." For nearly an hour, he had no idea whether she was alive and kept calling her without success. Then the phone finally connected and Yunisha answered. "Finally, my daughter received my call and I couldn't stop myself, broke out... two relatives that were with me also cried and hugged me," he said. Yunisha appears tearful as she recalls that moment. "After I had reached the top of the hill, I received a call from my father. He was tearful and I could not speak a word then," she said. Back home, her family waited anxiously for her return. "Even my younger daughter couldn't sleep. But I felt so good to see her after three days (Friday), I am so happy and relieved," her mother said. Yunisha says she is now thinking about what comes next. "Now I am worried about my further studies," she said. "If I had to change my school, I would have to miss my old friends and will face difficulties to make new friends. I am sad about my further studies." Head teacher Dawadi says better warning systems, including sirens and evacuation alerts, could have helped residents respond sooner. But he believes his decision to act immediately prevented a catastrophe. "Had I decided to close the school after the period, nothing might be left, only the bell would be ringing at 9:30." Photograph: Reuters Volodymyr Zelenskyy Ukraine hit by deadly Russian strikes as ‘thanks’ for Trump diesel deal, Zelenskyy says Ukrainian president says money from fuel sales will intensify war as European leaders reiterate support for Kyiv Oliver Holmes Sat 10 Oct 2026 10.45 EDT Last modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 12.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine as “thanks” for a deal cut by Donald Trump with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, accusing Washington of helping fund Moscow’s war. The Ukrainian president has expressed repeated outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue. The deal, which appeared to blind side Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president. He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”. That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 15 people, including three children. View image in fullscreen Rescuers working at the site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian strike in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Reuters “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday. “Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said. There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said. Map of Russian-controlled territory in Ukraine In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting ​an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”. “Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” ​ Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump. The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”. “This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist. View image in fullscreen Kaja Kallas with Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit in Copenhagen last year. Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/Reuters Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine . The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash Read more The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”. Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”. Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said ​on Saturday. Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same. Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The Financial Times reported that during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes. China Human Rights Human Rights Lawyer Applauds US Senate for Passing Anti-Forced Organ Harvesting Bill David Matas said the passage of the bill shows bipartisan support and sets an international example. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Human rights lawyer David Matas speaks at an event marking the 24th anniversary of the Chinese regime's ongoing persecution of Falun Gong, in London on July 15, 2023. Yanning Qi/The Epoch Times Alex Wu 10/3/2026 | Updated: 10/4/2026 0:00 X 1 After the Senate on Sept. 28 unanimously passed a bill seeking to address forced organ harvesting in China, David Matas, a renowned international human rights lawyer who has been investigating the Chinese regime’s atrocities for decades, spoke with The Epoch Times about the bill’s significance. The Falun Gong and Victims of Forced Organ Harvesting Protection Act (S.4009) aims to address the persecution and forced removal of organs from prisoners of conscience, largely Falun Gong practitioners, Uyghurs, and other religious or ethnic minority groups. It authorizes the U.S. government to investigate and impose mandatory sanctions against foreign individuals and entities involved in state-sponsored forced organ harvesting and trafficking within China. Matas pointed out the significance of the Senate’s unanimous passage of the bill. “That means that the legislation had support across the political and ideological spectrum,” he said. To become law, the bill still needs to pass the House of Representatives and be signed by the president. “Those are the next critical steps,” Matas said. Related Stories Organ Harvesting Bill Passes Senate Forced Organ Harvesting Bill Passed by Senate: What to Know Matas is one of Canada’s most prominent international human rights lawyers, having long focused on major human rights issues such as refugee protection, the prevention of genocide and hate speech, and exposing the Chinese Communist Party’s practice of forced organ harvesting. He collaborated with the late David Kilgour, a human rights activist and member of the House of Commons of Canada, to investigate allegations of forced organ harvesting from detained prisoners of conscience. Their 2006 investigative report, later published as the book “Bloody Harvest: Organ Harvesting of Falun Gong Practitioners in China,” has drawn international attention to the Chinese state-sponsored crime against humanity, and it won them a nomination for the Nobel Peace Prize in 2010. Matas has received numerous international human rights awards, including the Order of Canada. “The fact that the bill was adopted in the Senate now is an acknowledgment that the problem of forced organ harvesting with Falun Gong victims persists,” Matas said. The bill proposes sanctions on individuals involved in forced organ harvesting and organ trafficking, such as visa restrictions and asset-blocking measures. “[These sanctions] make sense only if one assumes that the abuse is happening. If it were not happening, there would be no need for the actions proposed in the bill,” Matas said. “Unless and until the government of China shows that the abuse is not happening, the assumption should be, according to the bill, as I understand it, that it is happening.” Falun Gong, also known as Falun Dafa, is a Chinese spiritual practice consisting of meditation exercises and the principles of truthfulness, compassion, and tolerance. It grew in popularity during the 1990s, and it had an estimated 70 million to 100 million practitioners nationwide by 1999, when the regime began a systematic elimination campaign. The number of practitioners detained over the years is likely to be in the millions, according to the Falun Dafa Information Center. Besides Matas and Kilgour’s works, other organizations have been investigating the forced organ harvesting from Falun Gong practitioners and other prisoners of conscience, including the World Organization to Investigate the Persecution of Falun Gong, Doctors Against Forced Organ Harvesting, and the International Coalition to End Transplant Abuse in China. American writer and researcher Ethan Gutmann also conducted a six-year independent investigation, interviewing more than 100 refugees, doctors, and law enforcement personnel. He published his findings in the 2014 book “The Slaughter: Mass Killings, Organ Harvesting, and China’s Secret Solution to Its Dissident Problem.” “The Senate would not have passed this bill if it did not take seriously the findings that researchers have presented over the years,” Matas said. “What makes the evidence so compelling is its combination.” Falun Gong practitioners demonstrate the exercises before a parade in the Czech capital city of Prague on Sept. 19, 2026. Zhang Qingqi/The Epoch Times Matas said Falun Gong practitioners have been disproportionately targeted within China’s organ transplant system for many reasons, including their sheer numbers. Also, their exercise regimen meant that their organs were healthy, Matas said. The Senate bill expresses an appreciation for the suffering of the families of the victims, Matas said, which will help surviving victims or victims’ families feel safer to come forward and share their experiences. International Impact Matas said Canada already has immigration legislation similar to the Senate bill, and the U.S. move will inspire other countries. The global Council of Europe Convention against Trafficking in Human Organs has only 16 ratifying parties so far, Matas noted. “Other states could and should join,” he said. The Senate bill could indeed serve as a “sorely needed” catalyst for action at the United Nations or other multilateral human rights bodies to take action, he said. Progress in stopping China’s live organ harvesting has been slow, but after more than 20 years of effort, “it is some comfort that, however long it took, this has happened,” he said. Liang Yao contributed to this report.
